text: Chapter 4, the rate limiter. Let's see how five algorithms decide who gets through, and who gets turned away.

A rate limiter is the doorman of your system. When too many requests arrive, it stops the extra ones at the door. That protects you from denial-of-service attacks, saves money, and keeps servers from overloading. A blocked request usually gets an HTTP four twenty-nine error.

Where should the limiter live? Not in the client. Users can skip your page and call the API directly. Put it on the server side, or in an API gateway. Every request has to pass through it, so that is the real gate.

First, the token bucket. Tokens drop into the bucket at a fixed rate, and when it's full, extra tokens are thrown away. Each request takes one token. No token, and the request is rejected. Say the capacity is five. After a quiet period, seven requests arrive at once. The first five pass, and the last two are rejected. Capacity decides how big a burst you allow. The refill rate decides the long-run speed.

The leaky bucket works differently. Requests join a first-in, first-out queue, and leave at a fixed rate, one at a time. Even a big burst comes out smooth. But when the queue is full, new requests are dropped, and the ones at the back wait a long time.

The fixed window counter is the simplest. Cut time into windows, with one counter per window. Under the quota, a request passes. At the quota, it's rejected. When the next window starts, the counter resets to zero. It's simple and cheap, and good enough for coarse rules.

But that reset hides a flaw. Say each window allows five requests. Five arrive at the very end of window one, and five more at the very start of window two. Each window is within its quota. Yet in about one second, ten requests got through. That's double the limit. A fixed window protects each window, not every stretch of time.

The sliding window log fixes this. It records a timestamp for every request. For each new one, it first removes timestamps that fell out of the window, then counts what's left, and allows the request only if there's room. The boundary burst is now blocked. The price is memory, because it stores one timestamp per request.

The sliding window counter is a compromise. It keeps just two numbers, the current window and the previous one, and weights the previous count by how much of it still overlaps the sliding window. That's the current count, plus the previous count times the overlap. It saves memory and smooths the boundary. But it assumes the previous window's traffic was even, so the result is only an approximation.

Each of the five has its trade-off. Need to allow short bursts? Token bucket. Need a smooth output? Leaky bucket. Want it simple and cheap? Fixed window. Need an exact rolling limit? Sliding window log. Want smooth and memory-efficient? Sliding window counter.

With several gateways, there's one more trap. Two gateways both read that one slot is left, both let a request through, and the slot is spent twice. The fix is to put the read, the check, and the deduction into a single Redis Lua script, so they run as one atomic step. One slot, one referee, decided in one go.
Remember three words: bucket, window, atomic. Buckets handle bursts and rate. Windows handle the boundary. And atomic operations keep many machines from overspending the limit.
